text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.

- Finland has underestimated the risks of joining Europe's planned monetary union, EMU, especially the possibility of external shocks to the economy, says Swedish professor Lars Calmfors, whose committee proposed Sweden should stay out of the 1999 start-up of EMU.
- Pensions should be determined by an employee's job history and retirement age, the finance ministry says suggesting restucturing the state's early retirement scheme. @
- Competition for ownership of regional power company Savon Voima heats up after cooperative Ita-Suomen Energia made a bigger offer than Swedish state-owned power group Vattenfall.

- Wage hikes of over three percent would weaken economic competitiveness and boost interest rates, financial market experts say, expecting a moderate two-year agreement from the next round of pay talks.
- The balance sheets of small and middle-sized companies are still too small, a report by Merita Bank and Finnish entrepreneurs federation shows. @
- Despite positive economic growth, unemployment will stay as high as 11 percent in 2001, the Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (ETLA) says.
- Finland's economy will be barely able to afford its aging population structure once the baby-boom generation retires by the year 2030, says finance ministry undersecretary of state Johnny Akerholm.
- Finnish tyre-maker Nokian Renkaat considering buying an unamed rival tyre-maker -- CEO Lasse Kurkilahti says there are several candidates for an acquisition. @
- Too few small and medium-sized companies have taken steps to prepare for transition to EMU, OKOBAMK chief executive Antti Tanskanen says.
- The Greens, Conservatives, Swedish People's Party and Chistian League will hold party conferences this weekend, and are expected to discuss topics ranging to EMU and NATO.
- The next pay settlement should be for a fixed period and should include support for employment, says the chairman of the municipal workers trade union. @
- Young Finns believe education is the best asset for those joining the job market, a study shows.
